questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q01

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Claim: Students should use digital calendars to track assignments. Which evidence best supports the claim? \

answer.text: A. Digital calendars can use different colors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This may describe a feature, but it does not prove the calendar helps track assignments.

answer.text: B. Calendars have existed for a long time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not support the claim about managing assignments.

answer.text: C. A teacher reports fewer missed deadlines when students record due dates in a calendar.

feedback.text: Correct. This evidence directly connects calendar use to assignment tracking.

answer.text: D. Some students prefer paper notebooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This may be relevant to a different discussion, but it does not support the claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 U06 L02 Q02

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Scenario: A speaker needs evidence about student reading habits. Which source is most reliable? \

answer.text: A. A social media post saying reading is boring

feedback.text: Incorrect. A personal post is not reliable evidence for an academic presentation.

answer.text: B. A random comment from an unknown user

feedback.text: Incorrect. The source is not verifiable or clearly reliable.

answer.text: C. A joke about students and books

feedback.text: Incorrect. A joke does not provide credible evidence.

answer.text: D. A school survey summarizing how often students read outside class

feedback.text: Correct. A school survey is relevant and provides usable evidence about the topic.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q03

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Which sequence is best for oral organization? \

answer.text: A. Claim, reason, evidence, explanation

feedback.text: Correct. This order gives listeners the point first, then support and meaning.

answer.text: B. Evidence, evidence, unrelated story, claim

feedback.text: Incorrect. This delays the claim and includes information that may distract listeners.

answer.text: C. Source name, closing, claim, new topic

feedback.text: Incorrect. This order is confusing and does not build support logically.

answer.text: D. Explanation, transition, unrelated fact, claim

feedback.text: Incorrect. The claim should come early so listeners know what the evidence supports.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.R.06 U06 L02 Q04

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Claim: After-school tutoring supports student learning. Which explanation best connects evidence to the claim? Evidence: Sign-in records show that tutoring attendance increases before exams. \

answer.text: A. Exams are part of many classes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is true but does not explain how the evidence supports the claim.

answer.text: B. Higher attendance before exams suggests students use tutoring when they need academic review.

feedback.text: Correct. This explains how the evidence supports the claim.

answer.text: C. Tutoring happens after school.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This repeats basic information without connecting evidence to learning.

answer.text: D. Sign-in sheets are made of paper or digital forms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This describes the record but not its meaning.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.W.02 U06 L02 Q05

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Claim: Students should learn how to check source credibility. Which reason best supports the claim? \

answer.text: A. Students need to avoid using inaccurate information in assignments and presentations.

feedback.text: Correct. This reason logically supports the claim and prepares for evidence.

answer.text: B. Websites can have different colors and layouts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Design differences do not explain why credibility checking matters.

answer.text: C. Search results appear quickly online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed does not prove that information is trustworthy.

answer.text: D. Some web pages have long titles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Title length does not show why source evaluation matters.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q06

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Scenario: A speaker gives three statistics but never explains them. What is the main problem? \

answer.text: A. The speaker has no evidence at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The speaker has evidence, but it is not explained.

answer.text: B. The speaker used too few numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. More numbers would not solve the missing explanation.

answer.text: C. The speaker used standard English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard English is not the problem.

answer.text: D. The speaker does not connect the evidence to the claim.

feedback.text: Correct. Evidence must be explained so listeners understand why it matters.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 U06 L02 Q07

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Scenario: A presentation needs evidence about school recycling. Which source is most useful? \

answer.text: A. A student's unrelated story about lunch

feedback.text: Incorrect. The story does not provide evidence about recycling.

answer.text: B. A rumor that recycling probably works

feedback.text: Incorrect. A rumor is not reliable evidence.

answer.text: C. A school recycling report showing how much paper was collected each month

feedback.text: Correct. This source is specific, relevant, and likely reliable for the topic.

answer.text: D. A picture of a trash can without explanation

feedback.text: Incorrect. A picture alone does not provide clear evidence for the claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q08

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Claim: A quiet study room would help students complete assignments. Which oral sentence best explains evidence? \

answer.text: A. The study room has walls and lights.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not explain how evidence supports the claim.

answer.text: B. The room is located near the hallway.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Location alone does not support the claim about completing assignments.

answer.text: C. Study rooms are rooms where people study.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is circular and does not use evidence.

answer.text: D. A sign-in log showing heavy use during project weeks suggests students seek quiet space when assignments require focus.

feedback.text: Correct. This sentence explains how the evidence supports the claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.W.02 U06 L02 Q09

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Which pair best shows claim and reason? \

answer.text: A. Claim: Planners have pages. Reason: Some pages are small.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not support why students should use planners.

answer.text: B. Claim: Students should use planners. Reason: Written due dates help students remember long-term assignments.

feedback.text: Correct. The reason directly supports the claim.

answer.text: C. Claim: Students use backpacks. Reason: Backpacks have zippers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason does not meaningfully support a position.

answer.text: D. Claim: Homework exists. Reason: Pencils write on paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is unrelated to the claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q10

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Scenario: Which sentence works best as an oral transition after giving evidence? \

answer.text: A. This evidence matters because it shows how the strategy helps students manage their work.

feedback.text: Correct. This transition connects evidence back to the claim.

answer.text: B. Anyway, that is a thing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is vague and does not connect ideas clearly.

answer.text: C. I found that online somewhere.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This weakens credibility and does not explain meaning.

answer.text: D. So, yeah, that happened.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is informal and does not guide listeners.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.R.06 U06 L02 Q11

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Claim: Student-led study groups can support review. Which evidence is strongest? \

answer.text: A. Study groups can meet in many places.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is a general detail, not strong support.

answer.text: B. Some students have notebooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not connect to study groups or review.

answer.text: C. A class survey shows students who attended study groups reported feeling more prepared for quizzes.

feedback.text: Correct. This evidence is relevant and directly supports the claim.

answer.text: D. The word group has five letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is unrelated to the claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q12

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Scenario: A speaker's evidence is credible but unrelated to the claim. What should the speaker do? \

answer.text: A. Keep it because all credible evidence is useful.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credible evidence still must support the claim.

answer.text: B. Replace it with evidence that directly supports the claim.

feedback.text: Correct. Evidence must be both credible and relevant.

answer.text: C. Put it at the beginning so listeners hear it first.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Placement does not fix unrelated evidence.

answer.text: D. Remove the claim and present only the evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The claim is needed to organize the presentation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 U06 L02 Q13

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Scenario: A student uses a source but cannot identify who created it or where the information came from. What is the concern? \

answer.text: A. The source is automatically perfect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Missing creator or origin information makes the source less trustworthy.

answer.text: B. The source must be used because it is short.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length does not prove reliability.

answer.text: C. The source should be used only as the conclusion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Placement does not solve a reliability problem.

answer.text: D. The source may not be reliable enough for an academic presentation.

feedback.text: Correct. Reliable sources should be traceable and credible.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q14

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Which sentence best introduces evidence in an oral presentation? \

answer.text: A. Here is some stuff I saw.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is vague and does not identify the source or evidence clearly.

answer.text: B. There are facts about this somewhere.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This weakens credibility because it does not name evidence.

answer.text: C. According to a school survey, many students use written reminders to track assignments.

feedback.text: Correct. This identifies the source and presents evidence clearly.

answer.text: D. You probably know what I mean already.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This assumes understanding and does not present evidence.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.W.02 U06 L02 Q15

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Claim: Schools should provide short research workshops. Which evidence best supports the claim? \

answer.text: A. Teachers report that students often need help deciding whether online sources are reliable.

feedback.text: Correct. This evidence supports the need for research workshops.

answer.text: B. Workshops can happen in rooms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is true but does not support the need for workshops.

answer.text: C. Research is a word with eight letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is irrelevant to the claim.

answer.text: D. Some students like computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not prove that research workshops are needed.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q16

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Scenario: A student begins with evidence before naming the claim. Why can this confuse listeners? \

answer.text: A. Listeners never need evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evidence is important, but listeners need context for it.

answer.text: B. Listeners may not know what point the evidence is supposed to support.

feedback.text: Correct. Oral presentations need clear organization so evidence has meaning.

answer.text: C. Evidence should always be hidden until the end.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evidence can appear early, but the claim should be clear.

answer.text: D. Claims are not allowed in oral presentations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Claims help organize oral communication.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.R.06 U06 L02 Q17

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Claim: Visual reminders help students remember deadlines. Which evidence is least supportive? \

answer.text: A. A classroom calendar shows upcoming assignment dates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This supports the claim because it is a visual reminder tied to deadlines.

answer.text: B. A student survey reports that many students check posted due-date reminders before leaving class.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This supports the claim because it connects visual reminders to student behavior.

answer.text: C. A teacher notes that written due dates reduce repeated questions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This supports the claim because written due dates are visual reminders.

answer.text: D. A poster in the hallway lists the lunch menu.

feedback.text: Correct. This is least supportive because it is a visual display but does not connect to assignment deadlines.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q18

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Scenario: Which sentence best explains why evidence matters? \

answer.text: A. The evidence is there and it is evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This repeats the word evidence without explaining its connection to the claim.

answer.text: B. This detail supports the claim because it shows students already use the strategy when assignments become more demanding.

feedback.text: Correct. This explains how the evidence connects to the claim.

answer.text: C. Sources are sometimes useful for presentations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is too general and does not explain a specific piece of evidence.

answer.text: D. My evidence is probably fine, so I will move on.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not help listeners understand the evidence.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 U06 L02 Q19

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Scenario: Which evidence choice should a speaker avoid in an academic presentation? \

answer.text: A. A school survey with clear results

feedback.text: Incorrect. A clear school survey can be a relevant and credible source.

answer.text: B. A teacher statement connected to classroom observations

feedback.text: Incorrect. A relevant teacher statement can provide useful support.

answer.text: C. A school report with dates and collected data

feedback.text: Incorrect. A dated report with data is generally stronger than an anonymous post.

answer.text: D. An anonymous post with no source information or evidence

feedback.text: Correct. An anonymous post with no source information is not reliable enough for an academic presentation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.W.02 U06 L02 Q20

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Claim: Students should prepare notes before presentations. Which reason best supports the claim? \

answer.text: A. Notes can be written in blue or black ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ink color does not explain why notes help presentations.

answer.text: B. Some notes are shorter than others.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length alone does not support the value of preparing notes.

answer.text: C. Prepared notes help speakers organize ideas and remember key evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. This reason directly supports the claim.

answer.text: D. Notes are pieces of paper or digital text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This defines notes but does not give a reason for using them.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q21

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Scenario: A speaker has a claim and evidence but no reason. What should the speaker add? \

answer.text: A. A sentence explaining why the claim makes sense before presenting the evidence

feedback.text: Correct. The reason bridges the claim and the evidence for listeners.

answer.text: B. A second unrelated claim

feedback.text: Incorrect. Another claim would make the presentation less focused.

answer.text: C. A joke that replaces the evidence

feedback.text: Incorrect. Humor cannot replace a clear reason in an academic presentation.

answer.text: D. A source title without explanation

feedback.text: Incorrect. A source title alone does not provide reasoning.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.R.06 U06 L02 Q22

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.R.06 Claim: Students benefit from peer review before submitting writing. Which evidence best supports the claim? \

answer.text: A. A writing teacher reports that students often catch unclear sentences after a peer asks questions.

feedback.text: Correct. This directly supports the benefit of peer review.

answer.text: B. Peer review happens during class sometimes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This states when it happens but not why it helps.

answer.text: C. Some students use pencils during writing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This detail is unrelated to peer review benefits.

answer.text: D. Writing assignments can be typed or handwritten.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not support the claim about peer review.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q23

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 Scenario: Which sentence would work best after presenting evidence in a speech? \

answer.text: A. That was the evidence, and now there are other things.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not explain how the evidence supports the claim.

answer.text: B. I found that because I needed something to say.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This weakens credibility and does not explain the evidence.

answer.text: C. This example matters because it shows how the strategy helps students solve the problem described in my claim.

feedback.text: Correct. This clearly connects evidence back to the presentation's claim.

answer.text: D. The evidence is finished, so I will stop explaining.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Listeners still need explanation of the evidence.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.RS.01 U06 L02 Q24

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.W.02 Scenario: A speaker uses a school survey and names when it was collected. Why does that help credibility? \

answer.text: A. Dates make every source automatically perfect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A date helps, but it does not make every source perfect.

answer.text: B. The audience no longer needs an explanation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credible evidence still needs explanation.

answer.text: C. It makes the presentation longer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Length is not the reason source information matters.

answer.text: D. It lets listeners understand where the evidence came from and how current it is.

feedback.text: Correct. Source information helps listeners judge reliability.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: MLA.ENG1.C.01 U06 L02 Q25

MLA Standard: MLA.ENG1.C.01 Scenario: Which oral plan is strongest? \

answer.text: A. Claim, unrelated fact, another topic, conclusion

feedback.text: Incorrect. This plan does not organize support around one clear point.

answer.text: B. Claim, reason, credible evidence, explanation of how the evidence supports the claim

feedback.text: Correct. This plan is logical and gives listeners a complete path through the idea.

answer.text: C. Evidence, source name, new claim, no explanation

feedback.text: Incorrect. This plan is incomplete because it does not clearly connect evidence to a claim.

answer.text: D. Topic, topic, topic, closing

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repeating a topic does not develop a supported oral presentation.
